lesson.title: The Upside Down Tree: How DNS Divides the World's Names
lesson.summary: DNS is not one giant database but a tree of delegated zones, root at the top, then top level domains, then the domains and subdomains people actually register.
lesson.body:
A single database mapping every hostname on the internet to its address would be a disaster to run. It would need constant updates from millions of independent owners, it would be a single point of failure, and every lookup anywhere in the world would have to go through it. DNS avoids that by never centralizing the data at all. Instead it organizes the entire namespace as a tree, and it hands each branch of that tree to a different, independently run set of servers. Nobody owns the whole thing, and nobody has to.

At the very top of the tree sits the root, represented by an empty label that is usually written as a trailing dot you never actually type. Below the root come the top level domains, or TLDs, things like com, org, edu, and country codes like uk or jp. Below each TLD come second level domains, the names organizations and individuals actually register, like example.com. Below that, the owner of example.com is free to create as many subdomains as they like, such as www.example.com or mail.example.com, without asking anyone else for permission. Each of these levels is a separate administrative zone, and each zone only has to know about the level directly below it, not the whole tree.

You can see the hierarchy directly by reading a domain name backward. Take www.example.com. The rightmost, implicit part is the root. Reading right to left, com is the TLD, managed by a registry operator under contract with a coordinating body. example.com is the second level domain, registered by whoever owns it and pointed at the name servers that person or organization runs. www is a specific hostname inside example.com's own zone, and example.com's administrators can add, remove, or change it any time without touching anything above them in the tree.

This structure is what makes the rest of DNS possible. Because each zone only manages its own small piece and simply points, or delegates, to the next zone down, a resolver can walk from the root to the exact answer it needs one step at a time. That walk, and the servers that make each step possible, are exactly what the next several chapters cover: the root name servers at the top, the authoritative servers that hold the real answers at the bottom, and the recursive resolver that ties the whole walk together on a client's behalf.
